This guy raises some good points about Triple A game companies in general. Personally, I think they're going downhill from here on. My hope for gaming lies within the indie dev scene. Yes, there are shit shows like certain early access titles(I'm looking at you in particular, Dayz), but games like Kerbal Space Program, Cities: Skylines, To The Moon, etc. has given me hope that anyone can make a game that can be amazing and fun.

From what I've noticed, most indie devs start out with good intentions, but are inhibited by their lack of knowledge about the gaming market. Kerbal is a great example of what could be done with the indie scene, but games like that are a rarity.

KSP is an interesting example, because of the company that made it.

They were not a game company at all. They were a guerrilla marketing company that made interactive advertisements. Which is kind of hard to explain if you don't know what it is. Basically, a company would come to them with a crazy idea for a publicity stunt, and they would figure out how to make it real. Think of those Bud Light "Up for whatever" commercials, but in real life.

Just because of the industry, the company was great at 2 things: Winging it, and convincing employers that they would get the product they wanted.

One day, their star engineer, who made all the impossible technical things happen, told his boss that he wanted to quit the company in order to make this video game he's been dreaming about making. Oh shit, this guy is like 50% of the reason the company exists. So they let him work on the game as a side project, as long as he didn't quit.

Then something happened and they realized the game could be a pretty good product. So it became less of a side project, more of a legit thing. Then the internet got a hold of it, it turned out to be really cool, and it became the main focus of the company.

Moral of the story: It was such a good indie game for 2 reasons. First, there was no significant pressure for the game to make money. It was only made into a project so they could keep the guy in the company for the real projects. Second, once it started to be good, the company was flexible enough to adapt to whatever situation the gaming market needed.

Sure, Nintendo doesn't always get everything right. And yes, some business practices are so archaic that even their competitors don't screw that up. But I think the reason people give them more wiggle room is because as a games publisher, they put out good, if not great, games. Everything is always polished, fun, and you never feel like you've been cheated out of however much you payed for their games.

Microsoft and Sony have no problem putting out some shitty title, or even a flagship title, with the promise of a day 1 patch because at the end of the day, they're not the ones who care about quality, just the bottom line. And in an industry where trying to be different is strayed away from so hard you'd think tripple A publishers thought the word "different" was another word for cancer, Nintendo has always been a breathe of fresh air in a world otherwise consumed by brown, grey, and bullets.

Sure, the Wii-U isn't the unquestionably superior console some people wanted it to be, but that doesn't mean it doesn't have any worthwhile games. The Wii-U is even capable of running titles at both 1080p and 60 fps. A task that it would seem like the PS4 and XBOne are uninterested in replicating even 1 of, let alone both. Which is further evidenced by the fact that publishers try to claim that 60 fps is pointless or detracts from their "cinematic" vision. Or how they lie and say their titles will be 1080p only to be at lower resolutions on launch.

Nintendo knows how to be different, they just have to be a bit smarter about how frequently to go about it. As far as consumers go, them being different is always a good thing. They'll innovate and bring the next trend with a dazzling new game. Their competitors can focus on being glorified Netflix boxes, but as long as Nintendo focuses on being a console first, we won't have anything to fear. I hope the next CEO has the same mindset, but will improve in the areas where Nintendo is constantly criticized.
